div.head: Mr. Landero to Señor Mariscal.
div.p: State Department and Office of Hacienda and Public Credit, Section 1st.

In relation to your communication of the 7th of February past, in which you inclosed a note addressed to you by the minister of the United States, who complained of the conduct of the employés in the maritime custom-houses toward American merchants and ships, inquiries have been instituted and particular attention has been paid to the points specified in the complaint made by the American minister in reference to the maritime custom-house of La Paz.
From the divers reports made to this department it appears that the said complaints are groundless for the following reasons:

Although it is a fact that a chess-board which belonged to the captain of a vessel was confiscated, it is not true that it was found in the cabin of the vessel; it was, with fifty-two packages, concealed in a bulkhead of the ship, and the entire lot, having been seized as contraband goods, was consigned to the judicial authorities, who condemned the said packages to be sequestrated.
It is generally understood that when contraband articles are seized the officers can make no exception of anything distrained, however insignificant its value may be.

With regard to the case of Mr. Ramirez, who received certain effects not protected by a proper consular invoice, he incurred the penalty specified by law for such an offense, and the officers were obliged to enforce it. The statement to the effect that the custom-house officials were unwilling to permit Mr. Ramirez to waive his claim is inexact, because the said gentleman, and also the firm through whose agency the merchandise came, abandoned their claim in conformity with the law, and the customhouse officers only fulfilled their duty by consigning the affair to the judicial authorities.

The statement that the captain of the bark Jupiter was permitted to land and sell clothing on which no duty had been paid) is not exact because the said bark arrived
in ballast from Mazatlan; when it anchored in that port it was searched, and when it was dispatched thence in ballast it had not on board the articles reported.

The notification given to the American minister to the effect that in Vera Cruz a fine had been imposed because certain invoices which they presented, while they contained a description of what the goods were did not state what they were not, is also incorrect.

In conclusion I desire to state that the custom-house employés entertain no prejudices against American vessels, nor against any others, nor would the government tolerate any abuses of the kind. The custom-house officials limit themselves merely to enforcing the laws, and punishing those who infringe them without regard to nationality.
This statement I have the honor to make, in reply to your above-mentioned official communication.
